column2: A Survey of Confidence Estimation and Calibration in Large Language Models (Geng et al.)
column4: What methods exist for estimating and calibrating LLM confidence, what challenges are unique to LLMs (exponential output space, semantic equivalence, prompt sensitivity), and what are the promising future directions?
column5: Survey covers: GPT-2/3/3.5/4, OPT, LLaMA 1&2, Vicuna, Falcon, PaLM-2, Claude, BERT, RoBERTa, T5, BART, PEGASUS, BlenderBot, GPT-4V, InstructBLIP
column6: References MMLU, HELM, HARNESS, various QA/MT/summarization/NLI benchmarks, unanswerable-question datasets
column7: QA (open-domain, extractive, MC), machine translation, summarization, classification, NLI, commonsense reasoning, dialogue, fact retrieval, hallucination detection
column8: Taxonomy: White-box (logit-based, internal-state probes like P(True)/P(IK), semantic entropy via entailment clustering) vs. Black-box (verbalized/linguistic confidence, consistency-based like SelfCheckGPT, surrogate models). Hybrid approaches also categorized.
column9: ECE (+ SCE, ACE, classwise-ECE, weighted-ECE), AUROC, AUARC, Brier score, reliability diagrams, Pearson correlation, Wasserstein similarity
column10: (1) LLM confidence estimation harder than discriminative models due to exponential output space, semantic equivalence, prompt sensitivity. (2) Combining information sources (logits+semantics, linguistic+consistency) outperforms single methods. (3) LLMs exhibit overconfidence — over-estimated tokens more prevalent. (4) Verbalized confidence often mismatches actual performance. (5) Discriminative calibration methods (temp scaling, label smoothing) don't transfer straightforwardly to LLM generation.
column11: No original experiments — purely a survey. Rapid pace of field may cause omissions. Predominantly English-language focus; no multilingual/cross-lingual calibration coverage.
column12: (1) Multidimensional benchmarks for diverse tasks, especially long-form generation with fine-grained annotations. (2) Extend to multimodal LLMs. (3) Calibrate to human variation/annotator disagreement rather than binary correctness. (4) Validate surrogate model approaches.
column13: (1) No systematic empirical comparison across the full taxonomy on same benchmarks/models. (2) Calibration for long-form/open-ended generation largely unexplored. (3) RLHF/instruction-tuning's effect on calibration degradation acknowledged but not deeply investigated. (4) CoT-induced confidence calibration across domains untested.

column2: Just Ask for Calibration: Strategies for Eliciting Calibrated Confidence Scores from LMs Fine-Tuned with Human Feedback (Tian et al.)
column4: Can calibrated confidence scores be extracted from RLHF-fine-tuned LLMs, and can verbalized confidence outperform model log-probabilities for calibration?
column5: GPT-3.5-turbo, GPT-4, Claude 1, Claude 2, Llama-2-70B-Chat. Also Llama-2-70B base vs. chat for RLHF degradation analysis.
column6: TriviaQA (1000 val questions), SciQ (1000 val questions), TruthfulQA (817 val questions)
column8: (1) Label probability (sampling-based conditional prob). (2) P(True) — sampling prob of 'True' when asked if answer is correct. (3) Verbalized numerical confidence (1-stage and 2-stage with top-k). (4) Linguistic likelihood expressions mapped to probabilities. (5) CoT variants. Key strategy: generating multiple hypotheses before assigning confidence ('considering the opposite').
column9: ECE, temperature-scaled ECE (ECE-t), temperature-scaled Brier Score (BS-t), AUC of selective accuracy vs. coverage
column10: (1) RLHF-LMs can verbalize confidence better-calibrated than their own conditional probabilities, often reducing ECE by >50%. (2) Generating/evaluating multiple hypotheses before confidence assignment (top-k) improves calibration. (3) Numerical probabilities work as well or better than linguistic expressions. (4) CoT does NOT improve verbalized calibration. (5) GPT-4 and GPT-3.5 show strongest verbalized calibration; Llama-2-70B-Chat less consistent.
column11: (1) Limited to factual recall tasks — unknown if results generalize to reasoning. (2) Closed-source models limit understanding of what enables good verbalized calibration. (3) Restricted to short-form QA — long-form generation not addressed.
column12: (1) What training factors enable well-calibrated verbalization (explaining GPT vs. Claude vs. Llama gaps). (2) Reduce sensitivity to prompt phrasing. (3) Whether short-answer calibration can improve long-form generation reliability. (4) Generalization to reasoning/arithmetic.
column13: (1) No testing beyond factual QA to reasoning/math/code. (2) No theoretical explanation of WHY verbalized confidence outperforms log-probs. (3) No calibration-targeted fine-tuning explored. (4) Stability across prompt formulations not systematically studied.

column2: Calibrating the Confidence of Large Language Models by Eliciting Fidelity (Zhang et al.)
column4: How can RLHF-aligned LLM confidence be calibrated by decomposing it into uncertainty about the question and fidelity to the generated answer?
column6: ARC-Challenge (1172 test), MMLU (1/8 subsample per subject), CommonSenseQA (1221 val), TruthfulQA (817)
column8: UF Calibration: decomposes confidence into (1) Uncertainty via information entropy of sampled answer frequency distribution over K samples, and (2) Fidelity via hierarchical fidelity chain — replacing chosen option with 'All other options are wrong' and testing if model sticks. Final: Conf = (1-Uncertainty) × F(ai). Baselines: Verbalized, Linguistic, Sampled frequency, Token logit prob, Conformal Prediction.
column9: ECE₁₀, IPR₁₀ (Inverse Pair Ratio — monotonicity of reliability diagram), CE₁₀ (Confidence Evenness — uniformity of confidence distribution), Brier Score
column10: (1) UF Calibration improves over baselines (Verb, Ling, Sampled, Token) on ECE/IPR/CE across most model-dataset combinations. (2) Robust to temperature variations (fidelity uses greedy decoding). (3) Fidelity alone provides strong calibration; Uncertainty alone insufficient. (4) Verbalization methods suffer from LLMs' preference for narrow fixed confidence ranges (0.8-0.9), worsening with model size.
column11: (1) Only applicable where answer set is known (MCQA, classification, preference labeling). (2) Fidelity in open-ended generation unexplored. (3) Requires multiple LLM invocations (K samples + 2-3 greedy calls per answer) — API cost concern.
column12: (1) Extend fidelity elicitation to open-ended generation. (2) Estimate token probability distributions with fewer model calls. (3) Develop framework for balancing ECE, IPR, and CE rather than over-optimizing one metric.
column13: (1) Untested beyond closed-form answers — open-ended/free-form QA not addressed. (2) No interaction with CoT reasoning explored. (3) No cross-lingual or domain-specific testing beyond 4 English MCQA benchmarks. (4) No unified framework for what 'balanced' calibration means across their 3 metrics.

column2: What Large Language Models Know and What People Think They Know (Steyvers et al., Nature Machine Intelligence)
column4: How large are the calibration gap (human confidence vs. model internal confidence) and discrimination gap (ability to distinguish correct/incorrect answers), and can modifying LLM explanations to reflect internal confidence reduce these gaps?
column5: GPT-3.5 (gpt-3.5-turbo-instruct), PaLM2 (text-bison@002), GPT-4o (gpt-4o-mini). 301 human participants via Prolific.
column6: MMLU (350 questions across 10 categories for MC), TriviaQA (336 questions across 7 topics for short-answer). Sampled for uniform distribution across confidence bins.
column7: MC QA (MMLU) + short-answer QA (TriviaQA) + behavioral experiments (6 studies, 301 human participants estimating LLM answer correctness probability)
column8: Internal confidence from token log-probabilities (normalized across answer options for MC; pTrue method for short-answer). Prompt-based uncertainty communication: explanations modified with low/medium/high confidence language aligned to model confidence.
column9: ECE (Expected Calibration Error), AUC via Mann-Whitney U (discrimination), Overconfidence Error (OE) in supplementary
column10: (1) Users consistently overestimate LLM accuracy — human ECE far worse than model ECE (e.g., GPT-3.5: model 0.104 vs. human 0.264). (2) Significant discrimination gap: model AUC 0.746-0.781, human AUC near chance ~0.59-0.60. (3) Longer explanations increase human confidence without improving discrimination (length bias). (4) Confidence-modified explanations significantly reduce both gaps (GPT-3.5 human ECE: 0.264→0.150; GPT-4o: 0.165→0.111).
column11: (1) Narrow question formats only (MC with few options, short open-ended). (2) Requires prompting LLM twice (once for answer/confidence, once for modified explanation). (3) Non-expert participants — results may differ with domain experts.
column12: (1) Broader/open-ended QA scenarios. (2) Single-step confidence-modified explanation generation. (3) Understanding fundamental causes of uncertainty miscommunication — why LLMs generate calibrated internal confidence but produce inconsistent explanations (hypothesized: RLHF preference bias + autoregressive choice-supportive bias).
column13: (1) No expert-user studies. (2) No real-world high-stakes settings beyond trivia QA. (3) Not tested on newer/open-source models beyond the 3 evaluated. (4) RLHF→overconfident explanations hypothesis untested empirically.

column2: Uncertainty Quantification and Confidence Calibration in Large Language Models: A Survey (Liu et al.)
column4: What is the taxonomy of UQ methods for LLMs across input, reasoning, parameter, and prediction uncertainty dimensions, and what challenges remain?
column5: Survey — references GPT-4 as exemplar. Discusses methods applicable to black-box and white-box models. Reviews LoRA-based methods (BLoB, BLoRA, LoRA ensembles) and LLM-as-a-judge paradigm.
column6: Table 3 organizes: Reading Comprehension (TriviaQA, CoQA, RACE, SQuAD, HotpotQA), Reasoning/Math (StrategyQA, GSM8K, CalibratedMath), Factuality (TruthfulQA, FEVER, HaluEval, FActScore), General Knowledge (MMLU, GPQA, HellaSwag), Consistency/Ambiguity (ParaRel, AmbigQA). Dedicated UQ benchmarks: MAQA, LM-Polygraph.
column7: QA (open-domain, conversational, multi-hop, MC), mathematical reasoning, fact verification, hallucination detection, reading comprehension, sentiment analysis, long-form generation. Applications: healthcare, robotics, transportation, legal.
column8: ~30 methods across 4 dimensions: Input uncertainty (input clarification ensembles, ICL-Sample, SPUQ); Reasoning uncertainty (TopologyUQ, CoT-UQ, TouT, UAG); Parameter uncertainty (BLoB, BLoRA, LoRA ensembles, SAPLMA); Prediction uncertainty — single-round (perplexity, SAR, P(True), entropy) and multi-round (predictive entropy, conformal prediction, ConU, HUQ, Semantic Entropy, Kernel Language Entropy). Also verbalized prompting and trainable estimators.
column9: ECE (primary), AUROC, AUPRC, AUARC. BLEU/ROUGE as proxies when binary correctness unavailable. LLM-as-a-judge evaluation.
column10: (1) Traditional UQ (MC dropout, deep ensembles) computationally prohibitive for trillion-parameter LLMs. (2) Multi-sample methods expensive (~$12k/million queries) with marginal gains (~0.02 AUROC). (3) Classical aleatoric/epistemic dichotomy insufficient — 4 uncertainty dimensions needed (input, reasoning, parameter, prediction). (4) Input and reasoning uncertainty notably understudied. (5) Standard metrics (AUROC, AUARC) fail to distinguish 'confidently wrong' from appropriately uncertain responses.
column11: Most UQ methods operate on single-round output — no multi-step reasoning chain support. Free-form NLG evaluation fundamentally challenging. LLM-as-a-judge subject to systematic biases. Cross-modality UQ (vision-language) poorly addressed — LVLMs show 2.4x higher uncertainty in visual vs. textual components.
column12: (1) Hybrid efficiency: low-cost proxies (attention variance, hidden state clustering) + targeted multi-sampling for high-risk outputs. (2) Interpretable modular architectures decoupling uncertainty sources via causal tracing. (3) Unified uncertainty embeddings for cross-modal settings. (4) Temporally-aware UQ for LLM agents with structured memory for cascading errors in multi-step reasoning. (5) Better UQ evaluation metrics beyond binary classification for open-ended generation.
column13: (1) Input uncertainty and reasoning uncertainty severely understudied — only 3 methods address input uncertainty in entire taxonomy. (2) No unified framework for propagating uncertainty across multi-step agentic reasoning. (3) Limited synthesis of which methods yield well-calibrated confidence across diverse tasks. (4) Relationship between overconfidence and specific uncertainty dimensions not empirically resolved.

column2: Mind the Confidence Gap: Overconfidence, Calibration, and Distractor Effects in LLMs (Chhikara, TMLR)
column4: Can presenting LLMs with plausible distractor options mitigate overconfidence and improve calibration? First large-scale study comparing free-generation vs. distractor-augmented prompting, disentangling effects of model scale, architecture, and fine-tuning regime.
column5: GPT-4o, GPT-4-turbo, GPT-4o-mini, LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instant, LLaMA-3-70B-Instruct, LLaMA-4-Scout-17B, Gemma2-9B-it, Qwen-qwq-32B (8B to >1T parameters, dense vs. MoE, SFT vs. RLHF)
column6: SimpleQA (4326 pairs), FaVIQ R-set supports (2922 pairs), TriviaQA validation (1000 pairs). Distractors (3 per question) generated by GPT-4o-mini, manually validated on 500+ samples.
column7: Factual QA in two settings: (a) free-generation (Normal/N) with confidence score, (b) distractor-augmented (D) selecting from 1 correct + 3 distractor options with confidence. Fine-grained analysis by question type (Date, Number, Person, Place).
column8: Verbalized self-reported confidence on 0-100 scale. Justified over token log-probs: captures task-level belief, more reliable post-RLHF, uniformly available across black-box and open-weight models.
column9: ECE with empirical binning (bin size 0.1). D_helped/D_harmed counts, relative accuracy gain, ECE compression between settings.
column10: (1) Distractors reduce overconfidence: up to 460% relative accuracy gain and 90% ECE reduction (GPT-4o ECE: 0.450→0.037 on SimpleQA). (2) BUT large RLHF models show INCREASED miscalibration on easy tasks under distractors (GPT-4o TriviaQA ECE rises 0.071→0.083 due to confidence inflation). (3) Small models (<10B) gain most accuracy but remain miscalibrated (LLaMA-3-8B ECE stays 0.36 despite 819% accuracy boost). (4) Person-queries hardest, highest ECE drop (69%) from distractors; Place-queries lowest (49%). (5) RLHF alone doesn't guarantee superior calibration — SFT-only Qwen outperforms smaller RLHF models.
column11: (1) Single distractor generator + single LLM judge (GPT-4o-mini) creates potential AI-generates/AI-judges loop bias. (2) Only verbalized confidence — no comparison with logit-based or consistency methods. (3) Results conditional on specific generator/judge pair.
column12: (1) Cross-model distractor sources and independent/human judges. (2) Targeted fine-tuning for specific question types. (3) Strategic model selection for deployment. (4) Integrating robust RLHF + optimized prompts + post-hoc calibration.
column13: (1) Limited to factual QA — no reasoning, open-ended, or multi-step tasks. (2) No comparison of verbalized vs. logit-based vs. consistency uncertainty methods. (3) Counterintuitive finding (distractors increase miscalibration on easy tasks for large models) identified but not explained. (4) Distractor quality/number effects on calibration untested. (5) No non-English or domain-specific (medical, legal) testing.

column2: The Consistency Hypothesis in Uncertainty Quantification for LLMs (Xiao et al., UAI)
column4: Does the 'consistency hypothesis' hold — when LLM generations for a query are more similar to each other, are they more likely to be correct? Formalizes and empirically tests this assumption underlying consistency-based UQ methods.
column5: Granite 13B, LLaMA 2 70B (QA), LLaMA 3 8B, Mistral 8x7B/Mixtral (summarization), Codellama 34B, Deepseek 33B fine-tuned with LoRA (text-to-SQL)
column6: CoQA (7983), TriviaQA (9960), Natural Questions (3610) for QA; CNN DailyMail, XSum (1000 each) for summarization; Spider (1034), Spider-Realistic (508), BIRD (1533) for text-to-SQL. Dev sets used.
column8: Three formal variants: Sim-Any (correct generations more similar to ALL others), Sim-Correct (correct more similar to other CORRECT), Sim-Separate (correct-correct similarity > incorrect-incorrect). Black-box UQ via aggregated pairwise similarities (arithmetic/geometric/harmonic means) over Jaccard, Rouge-1, Rouge-L, sentence-BERT cosine.
column9: AUROC (confidence as correctness classifier), AUARC (selective generation). For hypothesis testing: mean difference (Δ), fraction of verified groups φ(n_g) via one-sided t-tests at p≤0.05, maximum relative number of groups (ρ).
column10: (1) All 3 consistency hypotheses validated across 8 datasets/3 tasks — mean differences always positive. (2) Sim-Correct (H2) strongest but Sim-Any (H1) most actionable (no correctness labels needed). (3) Geometric/harmonic mean of Jaccard similarities outperform baselines (avg log prob, spectral eccentricity, p(True)) on AUROC/AUARC. (4) Hypothesis holds stronger for QA and text-to-SQL than summarization. (5) Stronger for few-shot than fine-tuned models.
column11: (1) Summarization shows weaker consistency effects due to higher correct-answer variability. (2) Fine-tuned models reduce correct/incorrect variability gap, weakening hypothesis. (3) Aggregated hypothesis has less statistical power than pairwise version. (4) Confidence evaluation limited to 3 datasets with simple aggregation functions.
column12: Investigation of other aggregation methods and broader empirical study with additional task complexities. Verification metrics and visualization tools can inspire new black-box UQ methods.
column13: (1) No tasks beyond QA/summarization/text-to-SQL (no reasoning, code, creative generation). (2) No calibration post-processing evaluated. (3) Relationship between consistency-based and verbalized confidence noted but unexplored. (4) No evaluation on frontier models (GPT-4, Claude) — generalization to SOTA proprietary LLMs unknown.

column2: Competing Biases underlie Overconfidence and Underconfidence in LLMs (Kumaran et al., Nature Machine Intelligence)
column4: How do LLMs update their confidence when presented with external advice, and what competing mechanisms explain the paradox of simultaneous overconfidence (reduced flexibility) and underconfidence (excessive sensitivity to contradictory feedback)?
column5: Gemma 3 12B (primary), Gemma 3 27B, GPT-4o, GPT o1-preview, DeepSeek-Chat (671B/~37B active), Llama 3.1 70B Instruct. o1-preview excluded from confidence analyses (no log-probs).
column6: Latitude dataset (~48k cities, 2000 questions per condition), difficult latitude variant (for GPT-4o/o1), SimpleQA (~4k questions converted to MC with 4 options), GSM-MC (MC version of GSM8k, ~9k math questions)
column7: Binary and MC QA in two-stage psychophysics-inspired paradigm: LLM answers, then receives advice from fictitious 'advice LLM' (stated accuracy 50-100%) and makes final choice. Key manipulations: Answer Shown vs. Hidden, Same/Opposite/Neutral advice, stated advice accuracy.
column8: Logit-based confidence from next-token distribution at answer position, calibrated via temperature scaling (T=3.3 for Gemma 12B, optimized on 40k validation questions to minimize ECE).
column9: ECE (for temperature scaling optimization), Brier score (0.15 for Gemma 12B), AUROC (0.88 for Gemma 12B), OUCS (Over/Underconfidence Score — signed weighted average difference between observed and Bayesian-optimal final confidence; positive=overconfidence, negative=underconfidence)
column10: (1) Choice-supportive bias: when LLMs see their initial answer, confidence inflates +0.22 and odds of changing mind drop 71%, even without new information — vanishes when answer attributed to another LLM (self-attribution dependent). (2) Systematic overweighting of contradictory information: LLMs update confidence ~2.0-2.17× Bayesian ideal for opposing advice vs. ~1.29× for supporting advice, producing marked underconfidence (OUCS=-0.30) under opposition. (3) Both biases generalize across all 6 models and transfer from factuality to math reasoning. (4) Pattern distinct from simple sycophancy (which would predict symmetric overweighting).
column11: (1) Binary/MC questions only — no free-form answers. (2) Code relies on Google-proprietary infrastructure, not fully releasable. (3) o1-preview lacks log-probs for confidence measurement. (4) No confirmation bias found, possibly due to ceiling effects (confidence >0.9 in Same-Shown condition). (5) Controlled conditions may not extend to naturalistic user-LLM interactions.
column12: (1) Test whether models without RLHF show different confidence updating patterns (RLHF may drive hypersensitivity to contradictory advice via sycophancy mechanisms). (2) Test for confirmation bias under different conditions. (3) Extend two-bias account to naturalistic free-form interactions.
column13: (1) No open-ended/generative tasks — unknown how biases manifest in free-form text. (2) RLHF vs. base model role in producing biases hypothesized but untested. (3) Iterative multi-round advice (beyond 2 stages) unexplored. (4) No mitigation strategies proposed or evaluated for either bias.

column2: Rewarding Doubt: A Reinforcement Learning Approach to Calibrated Confidence Expression of LLMs (ICLR 2026)
column4: Can LLMs be directly fine-tuned via reinforcement learning to express calibrated numerical confidence alongside their factual answers, integrating calibration into the generative process rather than post-hoc?
column5: Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct (4-bit quantized via Unsloth, LoRA fine-tuning). Ablations: LLaMA-3.1-8B, Qwen-2.5-3B, Qwen-2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B.
column6: Training: TriviaQA (single-answer), QAMPARI (multiple-answer). Generalization: CommonsenseQA, MedQA (both MC).
column7: Factual QA (single-answer and multiple-answer settings). Model generates answer + numerical confidence score (integer 0-10). Cross-domain and cross-setting generalization tested.
column8: Rewarding Doubt: PPO-based RL fine-tuning with logarithmic scoring rule (strictly proper scoring rule) as reward function. Reward increases for correct+high-confidence, penalizes incorrect+high-confidence. Optimal policy provably yields perfect calibration (Proposition 1).
column9: ECE, AUROC. Calibration curves (alignment with ideal 45° line) and confidence distribution histograms for qualitative assessment.
column10: (1) On TriviaQA: ECE=0.0226, AUROC=0.8592 — outperforms all zero-shot baselines and DPO-based LACIE; comparable to Trained Probe on ECE (0.0189) but superior on AUROC. (2) Generalizes to unseen domains — MedQA ECE: 0.4480→0.1145, AUROC: 0.5075→0.6649. (3) Mitigates overconfidence pattern (base LLMs cluster at 8-10) by producing wider, more calibrated distribution. (4) Does not degrade task accuracy.
column11: (1) Only tested on 3B-9B parameter models — no validation on larger models. (2) Correctness signal relies on rule-based binary metrics (exact match or F1 threshold) — extensions to LLM-as-a-judge or continuous NLG metrics not tested.
column12: (1) Extend to correctness signals from LLM-as-a-judge, reward models from human preferences, or continuous NLG metrics. (2) Apply to fact verification and free-text generation calibration.
column13: (1) Only factual QA with binary correctness — open-ended generation, reasoning, and tasks without clear ground truth untested. (2) Calibration-scale interaction (beyond 9B) unknown. (3) Well-calibrated statistical confidence may still mislead users in critical individual cases.
